hook_text: Every trig graph in matric is a radio with four knobs. Volume. Shelf. Speed. Start time. That's the whole topic.
clip_script: Every trig graph question you will ever see is a radio with four knobs. Knob one: volume. The number multiplying outside — two sine x — doubles how high the wave swings. Doesn't touch anything else. Knob two: the shelf. Adding one at the end lifts the whole wave up a shelf — now it swings around a middle line at one, from minus one up to three. Knob three: fast-forward. A number inside, against the x — sine of two x — plays the same song at double speed. Two full waves where one used to fit. And here's the trap the exam sets every single year: fast-forward does NOT change the volume. Faster is not taller. Knob four: start time. Sine of x minus thirty is the same song, pressed play thirty degrees late — every peak arrives thirty to the right. Don't read the sign; ask where the bracket hits zero. That's where the song starts. Now the party trick: start sine ninety degrees early, and listen — it opens at the top, falls, dips, returns. That's cosine. Cosine was never a different song. Same wave, earlier start. Four knobs. Every wave in the paper is just two of them, turned at once.
visual_style: A retro radio with four glowing knobs, each turn morphing a live sine wave on a small screen: taller, lifted, compressed, slid; the sine wave sliding left until it lands exactly on a cosine curve with a click.
mood: Cool, musical, satisfying — controls clicking into place.
pacing: One knob per beat, a sharp pause on 'Faster is not taller', smooth reveal for the cosine click.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take control of every wave in the paper.
